newsitem.title: USA: Multiple options seen for Brazil debt swap.
newsitem.headline: Multiple options seen for Brazil debt swap.

text.p: With the approval by a Senate committee to buy back external debts, Brazil is one step closer to making a splash with a global bond, U.S. analysts say.
As one of the options open to the Brazilian central bank, a global bond issuance can establish a benchmark yield while realizing savings on debt services, they say.

Unlike Mexico's fairly straightforward exchange of par bonds and discount bonds for new global issues, Brazil must decide on which bonds to buy back, said Vincent Palermo, Senior Quantitative Strategist at Merrill Lynch.

Brazil, which restructured loans later than Mexico, can choose from more than half a dozen Brady bonds which together have an estimated market valaue of $36.7 billion, more than twice the value of all Mexican Bradies.
"Mexico just did not have any uncollateralized bonds to swap with," Palermo said, "whereas Brazil has a well-defined Brady yield curve outside pars and discounts."
Buying back pars and discounts is unlikely to flatten Brazil's fairly steep spread curve, but it could shrink the spreads between collateralized and uncollateralized bonds, he said.

The goal is to establish a curve below the Brady curve, so that Brazil could continue issuing globals to retire Bradies. While the short-end may do well, demand for the long-end is uncertain, because the uncollateralized C bond is already out there, Palermo said.
Brazil C bond has a duration of 7.1 years, almost comparable to the 7.7-years duration for the 30-year Mexican fixed rate global.
Marcelo Fleury, a vice president at Garban Corp, expects a maturity of 20 years or more in a new global bond issuance.
"A new yield curve is crucial to confer a sense of trust and creditworthiness," he said.
The market has been abuzz with talks that the Brazilian central bank has been buying back external debt on the open market and might continue doing it, but Fleury took issue with the speculation.
The central bank, he said, is highly unlikely to go out on a limb in debt buyback, opening itself to attacks from various political parties, he said.
An explicit mandate is important for the central bank to actively manage the liabilities, Fleury said.
Since the Brady bonds are dollar denominated, a dollar global appears to make most sense, and the window of opportunity may be small while the U.S. rates remain low, Fleury added.
Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan and Merrill Lynch are said to be jockeying to lead the first Brazil global, according to market sources.
Brazil, with $58 billion in reserves as of July, could simply dip into its own pocket to retire the Brady debt, said an economist with a European bank.
Huge capital inflow since the real plan has forced the Brazilian government to offset the inflationary impact by issuing domestic bonds, he said.
The domestic interest rate burden could be lightened if the government has less reserves to sterilize, which, in theory, could also help solve some of Brazil's fiscal woes, the economist said.
